title: The Library Ghost's Missing Book
markdown:
The old library, peaceful by day, woke properly when dusk painted the sky lavender and indigo. For Ivy, the library’s gentle ghost, this was the best hour. She was not a rattling-chains sort of spirit. She was a soft sigh that moved the pages of old tales, a whisper of cool air through the dignity of the building. The papery smell of ancient stories was her favourite perfume.

Her dearest friend, Moth, a silk-wing fairy no bigger than a dewdrop, was often beside her. Moth left a faint trail of sparkly stardust wherever her wings carried her. Tonight they rested high on a shelf in the adventure section and watched moonbeams pour like liquid silver across the polished floor.

“Ivy,” Moth chimed, light as a snowflake landing, “where has The Lost City of the Sun gone?”

Ivy drifted closer. Her see-through form barely disturbed the dust motes. The familiar cover — gold, a forgotten land — was not in its place. “That is quite strange. It was here this morning, waiting for its next reader.”

A tiny frown on Moth’s brow. “No one checked it out. I watched Mrs. Gable put the returns away. The Lost City of the Sun was among them.”

Ivy sighed, the unfurling of a much-loved page. “Then it is a mystery. And a quiet night is a good time for one.”

They did not hurry. Ivy glided between the tall shelves, passing easily through solid wood, leaving only the faintest cool. Moth flitted ahead and lit the dim corners, pausing once to check a returns trolley that had nothing sun-coloured on it. They went past sleeping armchairs, cushions plump, as if holding stories of their own. The building settled: creaks of ancient wood, soft groans of foundations, the murmurs of a kind elder rather than anything frightening. In the poetry bay a window latch ticked, then thought better of it.

“Perhaps it rolled behind something,” Moth said in the history aisle. “Books are known to be a little restless.” She hovered near a stack of heavy atlases, worn leather, faded gold letters, maps of lands known and long forgotten.

Ivy drifted toward the children’s section, where colourful picture books lay together like a flock of sleeping birds. “Or it decided to go on a little adventure of its own. Exploring the lands it tells about, just for a while.” She paused beside a low table and a magnificent globe. Moonlight on painted oceans, deep calm blue; continents a soft green.

Deeper in, past stories of explorers and whispered legends, Moth’s light flickered. “Look.” Beneath the heavy shadow of a leather-bound volume titled Ancient Engineering Marvels, a sliver of familiar sun-drenched colour peeked out.

Ivy glided closer. There, tucked as if shy of the moonlight, was The Lost City of the Sun. Beside it, placed with care, a small handwritten note. Together they read the librarian’s slightly shaky hand.

To my dear Ivy and Moth. Please forgive the temporary move of this most treasured book. I needed its special knowledge for a very important project. The Inca people, you see, and their incredible rope bridges, those wonders made from the strongest plant fibres. Such marvels need constant care and renewal, much like the stories we hold dear within these walls. I will try to explain more fully in the morning light. It was signed, with a kind flourish, Mr. Abernathy.

Ivy’s second sigh was not mystery. “Of course. He was always so interested in how things were made, how they lasted.”

Moth’s wings made a happy swirl. “Inca rope bridges. Woven from plants. Pictures of them hanging across valleys. They had to rebuild them, didn’t they? New fibres, again and again.”

“Indeed. And he needed to study their making. Perhaps a new display. Perhaps he is learning the old art of mending something delicate.” The library, they saw, was not only a quiet place that held stories. It was a place that kept making and learning.

They nudged The Lost City of the Sun back onto its shelf. The sunlight on its cover seemed a little brighter, or perhaps that was only the moon finding the gold. Mr. Abernathy would have his explanation in the morning, and perhaps a new tale inspired by people who had known how to keep a bridge by remaking it.

Moonlight softened toward a pale hint of dawn. Ivy drifted to her favourite spot behind the grand reference desk. Moth settled on a dusty lampshade, wings dimming to a sleepy glow. The library went back to its deep calm. Ivy closed see-through eyes and listened to the building breathe. Soon Mr. Abernathy would arrive, and another day of stories would unfold. For now the book was home, the note was read, and the ropes in the pictures could wait until morning.
